rows.title: Paramount sells Simon & Schuster to private investment firm
rows.standfirst: Paramount Global has sold Simon & Schuster to the private equity firm KKR. The deal comes nearly a year after the Department of Justice blocked Penguin Random House from acquiring Simon & Schuster.

rows.title: What could break next?
rows.standfirst: Even if there isn't a recession right now, there are still vulnerable spots in the economy that could cause economic pain. Today on the show, we explore why some are concerned about the markets for commercial real estate and private credit.

rows.title: Trucking giant Yellow Corp. declares bankruptcy after years of financial struggles
rows.standfirst: The Chapter 11 bankruptcy, which was filed Sunday, comes just three years after Yellow received $700 million in pandemic-era loans from the federal government.

rows.title: Southwest employee accused white mom of trafficking her Black daughter, lawsuit says
rows.standfirst: When Mary MacCarthy and her 10-year-old landed at a Denver airport, two armed police officers were waiting to interrogate them.

rows.title: Ozempic and Wegovy maker courts prominent Black leaders to get Medicare's favor
rows.standfirst: Drugmaker Novo Nordisk focuses on Black lawmakers and opinion leaders to spread the message that obesity is a chronic disease — worth treating at a cost of $1,000 or more a month.

rows.title: 'Barbie' is the only billion-dollar blockbuster solely directed by a woman
rows.standfirst: Greta Gerwig's film joins a high-grossing list of mostly male-directed movies, most of them with men leading the casts.

rows.title: Musk vows to pay legal costs for users who get in trouble at work for their tweets
rows.standfirst: Elon Musk of X, formerly known as Twitter, said there is "no limit" on how much the company is willing to pay.

rows.title: Being in between jobs is normal. Here's how to talk about it
rows.standfirst: I recently went on medical leave from my job. I'm looking for a new career start and working through options. How can I talk about my in-between career state with friends and family?

rows.title: A tarot card reading for the U.S. economy
rows.standfirst: Predicting the future of the economy is always a dicey proposition. That is especially true after more than three years of pandemic-related economic weirdness. No one quite knows what will happen next.

rows.title: Farm Jobs Friday
rows.standfirst: Farm employment numbers are historically very hard to track. Partly because they fluctuate a lot from season to season, partly because a large portion of farm workers are undocumented. They're also not included in the monthly job numbers, which means we hardly ever talk about them on Jobs Friday. But today we're bringing you "Farm Jobs Friday" as we zoom in on three big trends in farm employment.

rows.title: The tension behind tipping; plus, the anger over box braids and Instagram stylists
rows.standfirst: Over the past few years, tipping expectations have changed: we're asked to tip in restaurants and coffee shops, yes, but also at bodegas, farm stands, even unmanned grab-and-go kiosks. And while the pandemic increased tips, inflation and a return to normal may put downward pressure on them again. Now, it seems none of us can agree on what the minimum should be. Host Brittany Luse chats with Ramtin Arablouei, co-host of the NPR history podcast Throughline , about the long and fraught history of tipping in the US, and what shifts in tipping may say about where we are today.

rows.title: The case for a soft landing in the economy just got another boost
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added 187,000 jobs in July, a slower but still solid pace of growth, suggesting the Federal Reserve may be able to curb inflation without triggering a recession.

rows.title: Hyundai and Kia recall nearly 92,000 cars and urge outdoor parking due to fire risk
rows.standfirst: Several Hyundai and Kia models are being recalled over faulty oil pumps that can overheat and cause fires — less than five months since the two automakers recalled vehicles due to another fire hazard.

rows.title: The U.S. added jobs at a solid pace in July, reinforcing hopes about the economy
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added 187,000 jobs in July, still marking a steady pace of growth. The unemployment rate edged down to 3.5%.

rows.title: Ex-Biden official's lawsuit against Fox echoes case that led to big settlement
rows.standfirst: Fox devoted 300 segments over an 8-month period to a disinformation researcher named Nina Jankowicz who joined the Biden administration. She says the coverage distorted her work and led her to resign.

rows.title: Breaking up big business is hard to do
rows.standfirst: The Federal Trade Commission is the sheriff for big businesses. One of its main functions is to stop companies from buying up other companies in a way that hurts competition. Those investigations have been going way up under FTC Chair Lina Khan, and it's not gone unnoticed by critics in business and some Republican lawmakers. Today on the show, we look at the FTC's scorecard under Lina Khan.

rows.title: Kansas newspaper says it investigated local police chief prior to newsroom raid
rows.standfirst: The Marion County Record had been looking into allegations of misconduct against the local police chief just months ago, according to the paper's publisher, raising concerns about their motives.

rows.title: Despite the Hollywood strike, some movies are still in production. Here's why
rows.standfirst: Hollywood actors are on strike, but the union is allowing some productions to continue. That's created some disagreement in the rank and file.

rows.title: A police raid of a Kansas newsroom raises alarms about violations of press freedom
rows.standfirst: Law enforcement officers raided the office of a local newspaper and a journalist's home. First Amendment experts are calling it a likely violation of federal law.

rows.title: Why lasers could help make the electric grid greener
rows.standfirst: Thousands of renewable projects are waiting to connect to the grid, but there aren't enough transmission lines. Some tech companies have faster and cheaper solutions.

rows.title: Silicon Valley's latest hype: Eyeball-scanning silver orbs to confirm you're human
rows.standfirst: The project is called Worldcoin. It was co-founded by Sam Altman of ChatGPT fame. Its mission is to authenticate all the world's humans, one eyeball scan at a time.

rows.title: The future of crypto hinges on a fight between the SEC and a former burger flipper
rows.standfirst: A looming courtroom battle between the largest cryptocurrency exchange and the world's most powerful regulator promises to shape the future of crypto.

rows.title: Amid streaming chaos, Dropout carves out its own niche
rows.standfirst: As big media companies struggle to become profitable, smaller companies like Dropout think they can make it work by offering niche content instead of going after a mass audience.

rows.title: Tale as old as time: Indicators of the Week
rows.standfirst: In a week jam-packed with major economic news, we've selected a few of our favorite stories for Indicators of the Week. Today we cover an Italian bank story, the drop in Chinese imports and the $1.6 billion acquisition of Simon & Schuster.

rows.title: The new Biden plan that could still erase your student loans
rows.standfirst: This summer, the Supreme Court struck down Biden's plan to forgive student loan debt for millions of borrowers. Except, on the same day Biden first announced that plan, he also unveiled another, the SAVE plan. And though SAVE sounded less significant than Biden's big forgiveness pledge, it's still alive and could erase even more student debt.

rows.title: Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried ordered to jail after judge revokes his bail
rows.standfirst: A federal judge has decided the disgraced former CEO of the cryptocurency exchange should be sent to jail as he awaits trial on fraud charges.

rows.title: UPS union negotiated a historic contract. Now workers have the final say
rows.standfirst: The Teamsters union reached a tentative deal with UPS, narrowly averting a nationwide strike. Rank-and-file union members are voting on whether to approve the contract.

rows.title: Coal miners say new limits on rock dust 'could save some lives'
rows.standfirst: Miners and their advocates testify in favor of new silica regulations aimed at preventing black lung disease

rows.title: The Titans' Terrell Williams temporarily will be the NFL's 4th Black head coach
rows.standfirst: Williams, who joined the Tennessee Titans in 2018 as a longtime defensive line coach, will step in for head coach Mike Vrabel during Saturday's pre-season game against Chicago.

rows.title: Beer in Britain's pubs just got cheaper, thanks to changes in the alcohol tax
rows.standfirst: The U.K. has lowered taxes on draft beers in pubs, in what it's calling its biggest shakeup to alcohol tax in a century. But taxes on other alcoholic beverages are rising, so not everyone is cheering.

rows.title: The echo of the bison
rows.standfirst: For over 10,000 years, many peoples in what's now known as North America relied on bison. Thirty million of these creatures stretched from modern Canada all the way down to Mexico.

rows.title: NPR's podcast and programming chief Anya Grundmann to leave after 30 years
rows.standfirst: NPR's top programming executive, Anya Grundmann, will leave at the end of the year. She has overseen numerous hits for the network, including Tiny Desk.

rows.title: Netflix extra DVD offer ahead of service shutdown confuses some customers
rows.standfirst: Fans of the streamer's 25-year-old hard-copy delivery service are welcoming the promotion ahead of its shutdown at the end of September. But the terms are vague.

rows.title: Opinion: Corporate ballpark names just don't have that special ring
rows.standfirst: NPR's Scott Simon ponders stadium naming rights: how relatively inexpensive it is for companies to link their brands to major league ballparks and football fields.

rows.title: Corporate DEI initiatives are facing cutbacks and legal attacks
rows.standfirst: Corporate DEI positions soared after the murder of George Floyd in 2020. Now, due to economic pressure and political pressure from the right, they face an uncertain future.

rows.title: Pickleball, the fastest growing sport in the country, is moving indoors
rows.standfirst: Pickleball is the fastest growing sport in the country. Indoor courts are popping up all over, from former warehouses, to empty stores and even shopping malls.

rows.title: Small Kansas paper raided by police has a history of hard-hitting reporting
rows.standfirst: The family owned Marion County Record stands out for holding local officials accountable. That role is becoming increasingly rare as local newspapers vanish across the country.

rows.title: After 19 years, the Tuohys say they plan to terminate Michael Oher's conservatorship
rows.standfirst: Lawyers for Sean and Leigh Anne Tuohy say the couple intends to end their conservatorship for Oher, a former NFL offensive lineman and the inspiration behind the 2009 film, The Blind Side.

rows.title: Metals, government debt, and a climate lawsuit
rows.standfirst: Last year, the Inflation Reduction Act was signed into law as the Biden Administration's signature attempt to combat climate change. Today, we present three climate-related indicators with guest Nate Hegyi of the public radio podcast, Outside/In.

rows.title: Europe gets more vacations than the U.S. Here are some reasons why.
rows.standfirst: Do you work more for more money? Or work less for more time? For some, this is the ultimate economic choice.

rows.title: The U.S. imports most of its solar panels. A new ruling may make that more expensive
rows.standfirst: The Commerce Department says solar panel makers in four Southeast Asian countries are evading U.S. duties on Chinese solar components. The finding could raise costs in the United States.

rows.title: Taiwan's companies make the world's electronics. Now they want to make weapons
rows.standfirst: As military tensions with China rise, Taiwan's companies are pivoting from civilian manufacturing to defense and weapons.

rows.title: New York City officially bans TikTok on all government devices
rows.standfirst: City employees will begin to lose access to TikTok and its website from all city-owned devices and networks, according to a New York City Hall spokesperson.

rows.title: When mortgage rates are too low to give up
rows.standfirst: The average mortgage rate in the U.S. just hit 7.09%—its highest level in more than two decades. And that's having ripple effects in the wider economy. Some homeowners feel locked in, tethered to their super low interest rates and unable to find something better. Today on the show, what happens when homeowners are locked in by low rates?

rows.title: Judge who signed Kansas newspaper search warrant had 2 DUI arrests, reports say
rows.standfirst: The Marion County Record now has all of the devices police seized in a raid. Local newspapers report that the judge who signed the search warrant had two drunken driving arrests within a year.

rows.title: A drought, a jam, a canal — Panama!
rows.standfirst: The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It sees hundreds of billions worth of stuff pass through it every year. But a historic drought is making it a little harder for big cargo ships to get through the fifty-one mile long channel. Today on the show, we look at how this backup presents yet another test for global supply chains.

rows.title: Political scientists confront real world politics dealing with hotel workers strike
rows.standfirst: The American Political Science Association, or APSA, is holding its annual meeting in Los Angeles this weekend despite calls from striking hotel workers for conferences to stay away from the city.

rows.title: MBA 8: Graduation and the Guppy Tank
rows.standfirst: Congratulations to the Planet Money Summer School Class of 2023!

rows.title: Summer School 8: Graduation and the Guppy Tank
rows.standfirst: Congratulations to the Planet Money Summer School Class of 2023!

rows.title: Young, "spoiled and miserable" in China
rows.standfirst: Every day, A Ze, a young woman in Beijing, would wake up early, do her makeup, and walk to her old work bus stop... and keep going. She'd left her job but couldn't let her parents know.

rows.title: Millions of additional salaried workers could get overtime pay under Biden proposal
rows.standfirst: A proposal from the Labor Department would make an estimated 3.6 million salaried workers newly eligible for overtime pay. It covers workers earning less than $55,000 per year.

rows.title: What's your MBA GPA? Take our Summer School final exam to find out
rows.standfirst: These 10 exam questions stand between you and a Planet Money Summer School diploma with your name on it.

rows.title: Hollywood union health insurance is particularly good. And it's jeopardized by strike
rows.standfirst: Hollywood actors and writers who qualify for their union health plans get a very good deal compared to other Americans. But not working during the strike threatens their eligibility in the system.

rows.title: On Maui, a desperate plea to tourists: Please return
rows.standfirst: When the deadly wildfires ignited on Maui, tourists were turned away. Three weeks later, business owners are eager for them visit — responsibly.

rows.title: Yes, people often forget to cancel their monthly subscriptions — and the costs add up
rows.standfirst: From streaming TV to razor blades by mail, Americans are buying more goods and services through pay-by-the-month plans. New research shows they often keep paying long after they want to.

rows.title: The problems with the US's farm worker program
rows.standfirst: Over the years, U.S. agriculture has grown increasingly dependent on the H-2A Guest Worker program to bring in foreign workers to harvest crops. H2A is a vestige of a U.S. and Mexican policy called the Bracero Program, which ended in the 1960s. Today on the show, why farmers and farm worker advocates are calling for more scrutiny of the current-day visa program, which has been dogged by concerns about worker exploitation and safety.

rows.title: There's a labor shortage in the U.S. Why is it so hard for migrants to legally work?
rows.standfirst: The wait time for an asylum-seeker in the U.S. to get a work permit is at least half a year. City governments across the country are pressing the federal government to change that.

rows.title: U.S. fines American Airlines for dozens of long tarmac delays
rows.standfirst: The U.S. Department of Transportation said Monday it is the largest such fine against an airline since rules covering long ground delays took effect about a decade ago.

rows.title: The Indicator Quiz: The Internet
rows.standfirst: What's hotter than a leather car seat in the late summer? The Indicator Quiz! We bring a listener onto the show and test their econ knowledge. Today's quiz is all about the Internet and artificial intelligence. Play along with us and see how you do!

rows.title: Armed with traffic cones, protesters are immobilizing driverless cars
rows.standfirst: Self-driving cars have flooded San Francisco's streets, and not everyone is happy. Street activists have been using a low-tech solution to incapacitate the vehicles.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
